observations.quote: A Secret indeed is to be concealed, it belongs onely to God to reveale it
observations.note: A secret is to be kept covered; revealing it belongs to God alone.

observations.quote: if it be disclosed, commonly it exposeth to death, or prison, or reproach
observations.note: Disclosure commonly brings death, prison, reproach, fear or exile on the one who discloses; the reason given for concealment.

observations.quote: unlesse we will brand our reputation with a perpetuall blur of lying and deceit to conceale the same
observations.note: The only escape named from those dangers is to cover the secret by lying and deceit, at the cost of one's reputation.

observations.quote: Lully; Arnold, Zachary of Paris, and others, are witnesses hereof
observations.name: Lully; Arnold, Zachary of Paris
observations.note: Named persons are cited as witnesses of what disclosure brings; no words of theirs are reported.

observations.quote: The true Hermetick Phylosophers took an Oath that they would follow the footsteps of their fathers and masters
observations.note: A group is said to be bound by oath to keep to their fathers' and masters' way and not to expose Nature.

observations.quote: the virginity of Nature, which hath been preserved from the begining of the world
observations.note: A figure: what the oath keeps from defilement is called Nature's virginity, preserved since the beginning of the world; not meant plainly.

observations.quote: yet have they bequeathed their secrets to their sworn disciples
observations.note: The secrets are handed on, but only to sworn disciples bound by faith and gratitude and made worthy by nature or education.

observations.quote: which yet are with much sweat to be searched out
observations.note: Even what is handed on must still be searched out with much labour; it is not given openly.

observations.quote: Without paines-taking none is fit to injoy that Art.
observations.note: The margin note makes labour the condition for enjoying 'that Art'.

observations.quote: that he approveth of no sort of Physitians, but that he would professe himselfe to be the sole and onely Physitian in all the world
observations.name: Men of shallow judgement
observations.note: A view of Paracelsus that the author gives to men of shallow judgement in order to reject it.

observations.quote: he only condemns the common rable of Physitians who are altogether ignorant both of Theory & Practice
observations.note: The author's own account of whom Paracelsus condemns: only physicians ignorant of both theory and practice.

observations.quote: Nor truely are they to be accounted Physitians, who Verbally and Syllogistically onely make a great flourish of Physick, but doe no cures at all
observations.note: Those who only talk and argue physick and cure nothing are denied the name of physician.

observations.quote: boasting that they have the Method of Physick
observations.name: they, who Verbally and Syllogistically onely make a great flourish of Physick
observations.voice: QUOTED: they, who Verbally and Syllogistically onely make a great flourish of Physick
observations.note: The boast of those verbal physicians, reported in order to be rejected.

observations.quote: Some of them are so incensed against that Theophrastus
observations.note: The man called Paracelsus earlier in this paragraph is here spoken of as 'that Theophrastus'; the paragraph uses both names.

observations.quote: they had rather let their Patients perish then make use of his prescriptions
observations.note: Some physicians, out of anger at him, would sooner let patients die than use his prescriptions.

observations.quote: the better they are, the more doe they undervalue them
observations.note: His medicines are despised for fear their effect would blemish the despisers' repute: the better they are, the more they are run down.

observations.quote: falsly charge the genuine Chymists that they have lost the right method
observations.name: the Censurers of Theophrastus, those fallacious Medodists
observations.voice: QUOTED: the Censurers of Theophrastus, those fallacious Medodists
observations.note: The charge of the censurers of Theophrastus against the Chymists, reported and called false.

observations.quote: who linger out the cure, and lengthen the disease by their compendium
observations.note: The author's own charge against those censurers: their short way draws out the cure and lengthens the disease.

observations.quote: tis plaine to those that have their understanding inlightned
observations.note: What follows is said to be plain only to those whose understanding is enlightened.

observations.quote: Paracelsus observed onely that method that was agreeable to Reason and Experience
observations.note: The author holds that Paracelsus kept a method grounded in reason and experience.

observations.quote: we are not so much to regard by whom, as what it is that is spoken
observations.note: Truth is set above any man's authority: what is said counts for more than who says it.

observations.quote: True Method consisteth in the knowledg of the Disease, and the Cure of it
observations.note: The text says what True Method is: knowing the disease and curing it, spelled out after 'viz.' as what food with fitting medicines drives sickness away.

observations.quote: Wimpeneus learnedly sheweth that greatest and most grievous Diseases now a dayes are in three respects cured by the Paracelsians
observations.name: Wimpeneus
observations.note: A named writer is given as the source of the three respects that follow (First CH5.32, Secondly CH5.45, Thirdly CH5.46).

observations.quote: in three respects
observations.note: Announces a numbered set of three, taken up as First, Secondly, Thirdly in CH5.32, CH5.45, CH5.46.

observations.quote: First, Because the Diseases are more perfectly known
observations.note: The first of the three respects: diseases are better known.

observations.quote: those that sprang from Tartar cleaving to any part could not be cured, because it cannot be referred to any of those four humours
observations.note: Diseases from Tartar could not be cured while all diseases were reduced to the four humours.

observations.quote: And since we are here fallen upon Tartar I will speak a little more of it.
observations.note: The author announces a digression on Tartar; it runs to 'So much for Tartar.' at the end of CH5.44.

observations.quote: The first Ens or Being toward life
observations.note: 'Ens' is given with 'or Being' beside it; the first Ens is that from which the body has its nourishment, arising from the last matter of the meat.

observations.quote: by the Archaeus, or digestion of the Stomack
observations.note: Here 'the Archaeus' is given with 'or digestion of the Stomack' beside it.

observations.quote: it's separation, and generation of separation
observations.note: The first Ens arises from the last matter of the meat by separation.

observations.quote: reduc'd unto Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt, as is plain in the three chief Emunctories
observations.note: Nourishment is reduced into three, Sulphur, Mercury and Salt; the body's three chief outlets are given as the evidence.

observations.quote: the superfluity of Salt is separated by the Urine, that of Sulphure is divided and purged through the Entrals
observations.note: Excess Salt leaves by the urine, excess Sulphur through the entrails.

observations.quote: Mercury or the moisture of that which nourisheth
observations.note: Mercury is here called the moisture of what nourishes.

observations.quote: if there be too much of it passeth through the pores by sweat
observations.note: Excess Mercury leaves through the pores by sweat.

observations.quote: Every member hath its own proper digestion, seperation, emunctory, excrement in it selfe.
observations.note: Each member has its own digestion, separation, outlet and excrement.

observations.quote: The first digestion of the stomack is not digestion, but apparation for the digestions of the particular members.
observations.note: The note denies that the stomach's first digestion is digestion; the paragraph beside it speaks of 'the Archaeus, or digestion of the Stomack'.

observations.quote: Whatsoever we eat and drink hath in it a mucilagenous, clayish, and sandy Tartar hurtful to our Health
observations.note: All food and drink carries a Tartar harmful to health.

observations.quote: the Stomack which is the instrument of Mans Archaeus, or the Internal, innate Chymist which God hath planted in Man
observations.note: The Archaeus is called the inward, inborn Chymist planted in man by God; the stomach is its instrument.

observations.quote: it seperateth that which is impure, dreggy, and Tartarous from the pure Nourishment
observations.note: The stomach parts the impure and Tartarous from the pure nourishment as soon as it takes anything in.

observations.quote: if the Stomack be strong in it's ful separative force, the pure passeth to the Members for nourishment, the impure goeth out by successe
observations.note: With a strong stomach the pure goes to the members and the impure leaves the body.

observations.quote: If the Stomack be weak and feeble the impure also is sent through the Mesaraick veins to the Liver, and there separated and digested the second time
observations.note: A weak stomach passes the impure on to the liver for a second separation and digestion.

observations.quote: seperateth the pure from the impure, viz. the Rubie from the Chrystall
observations.note: Pure and impure are given the names of two stones; the text goes on to say what each is.

observations.quote: The Rubie is the nourishment of all the members
observations.note: The text says what 'the Rubie' means here.

observations.quote: the Christall or that which is not the nourishment it sendeth to the reines
observations.note: The text says the Christall is what is not nourishment, sent to the kidneys.

observations.quote: this is urine, which is nothing else but the Salt pressed out of the Mercurialls, forced into resolution by the violence of separation
observations.note: Urine is said to be nothing but the Salt pressed out of 'the Mercurialls' by the violence of separation.

observations.quote: If the Liver be weak and cannot well separate it sendeth it to the kidneys mucilaginous and stony
observations.note: With a weak liver the matter reaches the kidneys slimy and stony.

observations.quote: that is, when the spirits of Salt, viz. of the flesh and of the urine are united
observations.note: The text glosses 'want of good separation' in the kidneys: the spirits of Salt of the flesh and of the urine are joined.

observations.quote: the Spirit of the Salt coming between by the power of predestination, it is coagulated into Sand or Tartar, either cloddy or mucilaginous
observations.note: When separation fails, the Spirit of the Salt coagulates the matter in the kidneys into sand or Tartar.

observations.quote: the second which is of the stomack into haile; the third of the kidneys and bladder into a little stone
observations.what: the first, second and third separation of Tartar
observations.note: The note numbers three separations of Tartar and what each turns into: mosse, haile, a little stone; the first stands beside a gap in the print.

observations.quote: the second which is of the stomack into haile
observations.note: The note puts the liver's separation first and gives the stomach the second; CH5.34 has the stomach separate first and the liver 'the second time'.

observations.quote: Every Man hath mosse & haile, but not a stone in him.
observations.note: Mosse and haile are in every man; the stone is not.

observations.quote: Tartar therefore is the excrement of meat and drink, which by the spirit of Salt is coagulated in Man
observations.note: The text states what Tartar is.

observations.quote: except it be mixt together with the Excrements by the proper expulsive vertue and so cast our with them
observations.note: Tartar is not coagulated in man when the body's own expelling power casts it out with the excrements.

observations.quote: four kinds of Tartar, the stone of the bladder, the Sand of the Kidneys, the clods or gobbets, as also the Slime or lutous matter of the stomack
observations.note: Four kinds of Tartar are counted and named by the form they take in the body.

observations.quote: with many other diseases which the Ancients knew not
observations.note: These and many other diseases were not known to the Ancients.

observations.quote: Paracelsus distinguisheth Tartar into that which is strange or forraine proceeding from meat and drink, and that which is innate of the cruor or hereditary blood
observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.note: A twofold division of Tartar, foreign from food and innate from hereditary blood, is given to Paracelsus.

observations.quote: which innate Tartarous disposition cannot be cured by the Physitian who knows not how to force Nature
observations.note: The inborn Tartarous disposition is beyond the physician who cannot 'force Nature'; whether this is still Paracelsus' teaching or the author's the sentence does not show.

observations.quote: but onely by the Quint-Essence of Gold which reneweth the whole body
observations.note: One remedy is named as the only cure of innate Tartar and said to renew the whole body; the lines given do not say how it is made, nor whether the claim is the author's or Paracelsus'.

observations.quote: Tartar therefore or the Naturall superfluity (the mucilage of Salt) is the mother of almost all diseases of all coagulate bodies
observations.note: Tartar is given two further names, the natural superfluity and the mucilage of Salt, and called the mother of almost all diseases.

observations.quote: hath Poyson or a Tartarous Mucilaginous Impurity hard by or close unto the medicine or Physick thereof
observations.note: By divine ordination every food has a poison, glossed as Tartarous impurity, close beside its medicine.

observations.quote: Paracels saith that the Matter, viz. the Tartar of diseases is twofold
observations.name: Paracels
observations.note: The margin note gives Paracelsus a twofold division of the Tartar of diseases, Bolous and Viscous.

observations.quote: Bolous, such as in milk meats, fish, and flesh
observations.note: Two named kinds of the matter of diseases, each with the foods that yield it: Bolous from milk meats, fish and flesh; Viscous from pulse, coleworts, roots, fruits.

observations.quote: There are four sorts of Tartar, springing from the fourfold fruits of the Elements by which we are nourished.
observations.note: Four sorts of Tartar are announced, by the fourfold fruits of the Elements; CH5.39 to CH5.42 number them.

observations.quote: There are four sorts of Tartar, springing from the fourfold fruits of the Elements
observations.note: This four is counted by the source of the food; the four kinds of CH5.35 are counted by the form in the body. The lines given do not say how the two fours relate.

observations.quote: The first sort ariseth from the use of those things which grow in the Earth
observations.note: First sort: from what grows in the Earth.

observations.quote: The second cometh from the nourishment which we have from the Water
observations.note: Second sort: from foods of the Water.

observations.quote: The third is in the Flesh of Beasts and Fowles.
observations.note: Third sort: in the flesh of beasts and fowls; no element is named in this line.

observations.quote: The fourth from the Firmament, which is most like to the Spirit of wine in its subtilty
observations.note: Fourth sort: from the Firmament, likened to Spirit of wine for subtlety and said to have the strongest impression.

observations.quote: if the Aire be infected by the vapours of the Earth, and Water, and Firmament, afterward it affecteth us also
observations.note: The air, infected by vapours of Earth, Water and Firmament, then affects men.

observations.quote: those acute and pernicious Astrall diseases, the Pleuresie, Plague
observations.note: A class of diseases is named 'Astrall' and examples given.

observations.quote: which diseases proceeding from the impressions of the Stars the universall medicine powerfull expelleth
observations.note: A thing named 'the universall medicine' is said to expel the diseases from the impressions of the Stars; the lines given do not say what it is.

observations.quote: Those four kinds of Tartar shew themselves in the Urine, and are judged of by the art of separation
observations.note: The kind of Tartar behind a disease is judged in the urine by the art of separation.

observations.quote: He that knoweth what sort of food any one eateth, may also know his disease
observations.note: Food and disease are each knowable from the other.

observations.quote: The disease is cured by the same Element that was the cause of it.
observations.note: A rule of cure: by the same Element that caused the disease.

observations.quote: which Paracelsus comprehendeth under the name of Poyson and Tartar
observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.note: The excrements of meat and drink are what Paracelsus means by the names Poyson and Tartar.

observations.quote: Choller and Melancholly had long since been rooted out of the Physitians Garden
observations.note: Had Galen and his followers known these excrements, Choler and Melancholy would long since have been given up; said in the figure of a garden.

observations.quote: cannot possibly understand how the Author of diseases afflicteth us, by destroying the frame of the little world and taking away our life
observations.note: Without knowing the Tartarous matter one cannot understand how 'the Author of diseases' afflicts us; the Author of diseases is not named.

observations.quote: by destroying the frame of the little world
observations.note: Man is called the little world.

observations.quote: our Naturall Heat, or the microcosmicall heat of the Sun and Moon that is in us
observations.note: What separates Tartar from nourishment is named: our natural heat, also called the microcosmical heat of the Sun and Moon in us, which digests the nutriment.

observations.quote: the microcosmicall heat of the Sun and Moon that is in us
observations.note: 'Sun and Moon' are here spoken of as within man, not as the lights of the sky.

observations.quote: then it must be strengthned by its like, that is, by the macrocosmicall Heat of Sun and Moon, if it could be got
observations.note: Weakened inner heat is to be strengthened by its like in the great world; 'if it could be got' marks it as hard to come by.

observations.quote: even the most simple matter which the most Great God generated of the spirit of the world (one and the same with the spirit of our body)
observations.note: A matter is pointed to but not named; the text says only what it is made of and that it is for restoring and keeping human nature.

observations.quote: the spirit of the world (one and the same with the spirit of our body)
observations.note: The spirit of the world and the spirit of man's body are said to be one and the same.

observations.quote: is deduced by art into act, viz. turned into such a simple spirit as is the spirit of our life, which is done by resolution and conjuction with the Nutriment
observations.note: Things holding the power of Sun and Moon are brought by art into act, turned into a simple spirit like the spirit of life, by resolution and joining with the nutriment.

observations.quote: The Vitall spirit in Man and the Elementall is but one spirit.
observations.note: The note makes the vital spirit in man and the elemental spirit one.

observations.quote: then the excrements stay in the Chylus, and cause stomachall diseases in the stomack, Jecorall in the liver
observations.note: If the separating Archaeus of stomach, liver or kidneys is infected or hindered, the excrements stay in the Chylus and breed the diseases of each place.

observations.quote: and breed the Gout in the hands, feet, knees, from congelation of the glew by the spirit of Salt
observations.note: The Gout is said to come from the congealing of 'the glew' by the spirit of Salt.

observations.quote: Tartar differeth according to the places of the bodies pores and passages
observations.what: Tartar by places of the body
observations.note: Tartar is distinguished by where it lodges in the body; the note lists the places.

observations.quote: Therefore the Archaeus of the stomack must destroy the Tartar of the Elements least it be turned into the Tartar of Man
observations.what: the Tartar of the Elements; the Tartar of Man
observations.note: Two Tartars are set apart by name: the Tartar of the Elements and the Tartar of Man.

observations.quote: the spirit of the Sun which is Lord and Master of coagulation in various subjects will breed the Stone
observations.note: The spirit of the Sun is made lord of coagulation; in this context the Stone it breeds is the stone in the body.

observations.quote: the spirit of the Sun which is Lord and Master of coagulation in various subjects will breed the Stone
observations.note: Here the spirit of the Sun is lord of coagulation and breeds the Stone; CH5.35 has Tartar coagulated in man by the spirit of Salt. The lines given do not say how the two relate.

observations.quote: So much for Tartar.
observations.note: Closes the digression on Tartar opened at the end of CH5.32.

observations.quote: Secondly, Because we have more perfect medicines now then heretofore, that is to say, of Mineralls
observations.note: The second of the three respects: more perfect medicines, of minerals.

observations.quote: those skilfull Chymists the Sons of Cadmus
observations.note: The Chymists to whom the preparing of mineral medicines was discovered are given a figurative name the text does not explain.

observations.quote: A knotty piece must be cloven with hard wedges
observations.note: A saying about wood is used for diseases and remedies; the paragraph says its sense plainly: extreme diseases call for extreme remedies.

observations.quote: Paracelsus would have a steely medicine applied as proper for an iron disease
observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.note: A rule of cure given to Paracelsus: a steely medicine for an iron disease.

observations.quote: Thirdly, Because now the Harmony between the great and little world is made so plaine
observations.note: The third respect: the harmony of the great and the little world is now plainly understood.

observations.quote: as Silver, Saphir, Vitrioll, Emeralds, for the braine; for the heart, Gold, Pearles, Saffron; for the lungs, Brimstone
observations.note: From that harmony it is easy to know which medicine is familiar and friendly to which member; three members are given with their medicines.

observations.quote: Whereas Paracelsus offendeth Galen, Galen did the same to others
observations.note: Disagreement is common among physicians, not peculiar to Paracelsus: Galen went against others too.

observations.quote: Hippocrates wrote many things, which most Galenists reject at this day
observations.note: Most Galenists are said to reject much of what Hippocrates wrote.

observations.quote: nor doe the stoutest of common vulgar Physitians agree among themselves
observations.note: The common physicians do not agree with one another.

observations.quote: by those that differ in their most pugnacious opinions, and that are ignorant Mechanick forgers of diseases
observations.note: The author's words for the disputing physicians.

observations.quote: As between Schekius and Fuchsius about the continent Cause of diseases.
observations.note: First of five disputes named as examples: Schekius and Fuchsius; no words of theirs are reported.

observations.quote: Between Argenterius and Fernelius about Agues and Fevers.
observations.note: Second dispute named: Argenterius and Fernelius; no words of theirs are reported.

observations.quote: Between Galen and Rondeletius concerning the Palsie, Epilepsie and Stone.
observations.note: Third dispute named: Galen and Rondeletius; no words of theirs are reported.

observations.quote: Between Francaneianus, Rondelatius and Fallopius about the French Pox.
observations.note: Fourth dispute named; the second name is spelled 'Rondelatius' here and 'Rondeletius' in the sentence before.

observations.quote: Between Altomarus and Fernelius concerning the Gout.
observations.note: Fifth dispute named: Altomarus and Fernelius; no words of theirs are reported.

observations.quote: You may find more jarring in opinions in Agryppa
observations.name: Agryppa
observations.note: The note sends the reader to a named writer's chapter on medicine for more disagreements; part of the title stands at a gap. No words of his are given.

observations.quote: How many millions, according to the disagreeing and jarring method of these men, will still perish
observations.note: Many will die before these physicians settle the cause of the diseases they dispute.

observations.quote: I willingly passe by the Herbarists, who commonly squabble and raile at one another with endlesse jangling about the Wool of Plants
observations.note: The author passes over the quarrelsome Herbarists for brevity.

observations.quote: I exhort and admonish all Students of Hippocraticall and Galenicall Physick, in whom the Philosophicall veine is yet warme
observations.what: I exhort and admonish all Students of Hippocraticall and Galenicall Physick
observations.note: The author names whom he addresses and announces an exhortation to students of the old physic.

observations.quote: what our industry hath found out should not shut the door against that of the Ancients
observations.note: The students addressed are those who hold that new findings should not shut out the Ancients'.

observations.quote: that they would forsake their Fathers faults and other mens errours
observations.note: First thing urged: to leave inherited faults and others' errors.

observations.quote: spend some time in reading the works of this new Phylosopher and Physitian, not superficially and prefunctorily, but with greatest diligence and attention of mind
observations.note: Second thing urged: to read the works of this new philosopher and physician with the greatest care.

observations.quote: we are to imitate the experience and industry of the Bees
observations.note: The way to read is given in a figure: as bees gather, segregating the best from the worst.

observations.quote: I doe not so far perswade men that they should so adore every thing of Paracelsus
observations.note: The author limits his exhortation: Paracelsus is not to be taken as if all were Gospel-Oracles.

observations.quote: he himselfe hath recanted something of his over hasty writings
observations.note: Paracelsus himself is said to have taken back some of his over-hasty writings; no words of his are given.

observations.quote: as we see many who even worship the conclusions, and opinions of Hethen Authors
observations.note: Beside this the author sets the many who worship the opinions of heathen authors.

observations.quote: the diligent and accurate reading of him may give us greater light, and be no small advantage to us for the more intimate and right understanding of Hippocrates his works
observations.note: The reason given for reading Paracelsus: more light, and a better understanding of Hippocrates' works.

observations.quote: They are not to be praised who rashly condemn all that Paracelsus hath written, when yet they have not read so much as his marginall notes
observations.note: Those who condemn all of Paracelsus have not read even his margin notes.

observations.quote: or if they have, yet truly they understand not fully the third part of them
observations.note: Those who have read them are said not to understand a third of them.

observations.quote: throw away the kernell and pick up onely the husks of Phylosophers
observations.note: Those addressed as Phylosopasters keep the husk and throw away the kernel: an outer and an inner part of the philosophers' writings.

observations.quote: for the spirit, that ye may understand the dead letter of Theophrastus, and the Phylosophers
observations.note: The letter of Theophrastus and the philosophers is called dead; understanding it needs the spirit, to be asked of God.

observations.quote: His works which were Printed for the publick good, by the incouragement and at the cost of that most Renowned and Reverend Ernestus Prince Elector of Coleine
observations.note: The printing of Paracelsus' works is named, with the prince who encouraged and paid for it.

observations.quote: have given occasion to his adversaries to charge him with implicite and evident contradiction
observations.name: his adversaries
observations.note: The charge of contradiction is given to Paracelsus' adversaries; the author answers it by his manner of writing.

observations.quote: to the unskilfull and unlearned he wrote in a Magicall stile; not for the vulgar sort, but for himselfe and the understanding children of Wisdome trained up in the School of Magick
observations.note: The cause given for the seeming contradiction: he wrote in a magical style, for himself and the children of Wisdom, not for the common sort.

observations.quote: not for the Sophisticall Alchymists, such as are bewitch'd with a greedy desire of Gold
observations.note: A second group shut out: the Sophisticall Alchymists greedy for gold.

observations.quote: incensed with a righteous hatred against some most wretched, wicked, inhumane Physitians and Druggists of his time
observations.note: A motive given for his manner of writing: righteous hatred of physicians and druggists who often lay in wait to poison him.

observations.quote: those circumforanceous and vulgar Alchymists would have surpassed all other Physitians, and prostituted the Art
observations.note: Had he written more plainly, the vulgar alchemists would have outdone all physicians and made the Art common: the reason for not writing plainly.

observations.quote: He concealed his mysteries under vulgar and various names
observations.note: Stated: Paracelsus hid his mysteries under common and varied names.

observations.quote: we must not take the similitudes for the truth it selfe, or that which is intended by them
observations.note: A rule of reading: his likenesses are not the thing meant by them.

observations.quote: the Physicall Secrets, that is, the hidden power of God, or the Magicall WORDS in Paracelsus
observations.note: The text says what the Physicall Secrets are: the hidden power of God, or the magical words in Paracelsus.

observations.quote: they need and require a Delian swimmer, a most acute and sharp wit, a Magicall Understanding, even that purified eye of the Mind
observations.note: Few understand; the reader needs a special wit to search out the hidden sentences and mysteries.

observations.quote: I mean that which is True and lawfull
observations.note: The author says what he means by Magick everywhere; the word itself stands at a gap in the print.

observations.quote: which is fit for none but Vulcan, and deserveth to be burned
observations.note: What he does not mean: the infamous and profane kind (a word in foreign script, not given) or witchcraft, fit for the fire.

observations.quote: the absolute perfection of the whole most noble Phylosophy, the chiefest Wisdome of Gods works and the plenary knowledge of occult Nature
observations.note: What true Magick is.

observations.quote: by a fit application of Agents and Patients, observing the consent and dissent of things
observations.note: How Magick works its wonders beyond the usual order of Nature.

observations.quote: Paracelsus hath joyned the exercetation of either medicine together, as well that of Physick as of Chyrurgie, in imitation and after the example of Great Hippocrates
observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.note: The author reports that Paracelsus joined physick and surgery, following Hippocrates; no words of his are given.

observations.quote: a twofold Medicine, Physicall or the knowledge of all diseases, and Chyrurgicall or the curing of the same
observations.note: The two medicines are defined: Physicall the knowledge of diseases, Chyrurgicall the curing of them; the 'he' who set them down may be Paracelsus or Hippocrates.

observations.quote: Nor can either without the other safely consist or be exercised but with great hurt and danger of the sick
observations.note: Neither can be practised without the other without danger to the sick.

observations.quote: it is necessary that every Surgeon should be a Physician, and every Physitian a Chyrurgion
observations.note: The two must be one person.

observations.quote: that there may be a sound Bridgroom for a sound Bride
observations.note: The joining of the two in one man is put in the figure of bridegroom and bride.

observations.quote: their preparations and compositions made by the Physitian himselfe, and not carelesly left to others
observations.note: The physician himself must prepare and compound the medicines.

observations.quote: by their own hand to prepare the medicaments which they know, to seperate and purge them from their poyson and dreggs, to reduce them to their pure simplicity
observations.note: The work of the genuine physician: with his own hand to prepare the medicines, part them from poison and dregs, bring them to pure simplicity.

observations.quote: For the Bad and Good are mixt together, neither is Sugar free from faeculent impurity, nor is honey voyd of a venemous bitternesse
observations.note: The reason given: good and bad are mixed in things, even in sugar and honey; hence the need of separation.

observations.quote: he must with true faith and acurate skill or judgement accommodate them to mans necessities, that the root of the disease may be plucked up
observations.note: After preparing, the medicines are to be fitted to the patient's need so that the root of the disease is removed.

observations.quote: judgement without practice is altogether barren and fruitlesse
observations.note: A physician needs theory and practice together.

observations.quote: Physick is learned by the labour of the hands and practicall working or making it up, when the Fire discovereth new and most pleasant Remedies continually
observations.note: Physick is learned by handwork, and the Fire uncovers new remedies continually.

observations.quote: which Nature dayly more and more purgeth from their superfluities, and then delivereth them to her Servant to make them up
observations.note: Nature cleanses the remedies and hands them to her Servant; the chapter title calls the physician Natures Minister.

observations.quote: will not become schollers and school-boyes againe, to dig they are ashamed
observations.note: The great doctors grown grey in common physick refuse to learn handwork.

observations.quote: so these men will openly contradict the truth, and with a canine obstinate bawling bark at it
observations.note: Likened to an old tree and an old dog, they oppose the truth rather than mend their errors.

observations.quote: they exclaime and cry out against the Chymists as if they were no Physitians
observations.name: these Rationall Physitians
observations.note: The charge of the Rationall Physitians against the Chymists, reported by the author, who adds that the Chymists are the most skilful of any.

observations.quote: that they are the onely Physitians who in judgement and Reason (undervaluing Chymistry) know how to apply any Remedy to every disease
observations.name: these Rationall Physitians
observations.note: Their claim for themselves, reported in order to be rejected.

observations.quote: because they can prepare their medicines but onely with their Reason, not at all with their hand
observations.note: Why the rational physicians stand helpless at the sick bed: they prepare with reason only, not with the hand.

observations.quote: Yet here I will by no means undertake to defend them, who reteining the works of Hippocrates and of the Ancients, yet boast themselves to be the Schollers of Paracelsus
observations.note: The author refuses to defend those who keep the Ancients and yet call themselves scholars of Paracelsus.

observations.quote: but neither acknowledge the minde of the Author in his Theory, nor doe any thing praise-worthy in Practice
observations.note: His charge against them: they grasp neither the author's theory nor achieve anything in practice.

observations.quote: These Receits being lost by chance, all the Wisdome vanisheth from them
observations.note: Those whose wisdom lies in receipts lose it all when these are lost.

observations.quote: Experience, without Phylosophy the mother of Experience is uncertaine.
observations.note: Philosophy is called the mother of experience; experience without it is uncertain.

observations.quote: There are also false and lying Theophrasteans prophaning by their avarice and timerity that Divine Physick
observations.note: A further group is named and set apart: false Theophrasteans who profane that Divine Physick.

observations.quote: who under disguised names vaunt and vapour that they make use of Theophrastus his medicines
observations.name: false and lying Theophrasteans
observations.note: Their boast of using Theophrastus' medicines under disguised names, reported in order to be rejected.

observations.quote: being altogether ignorant not onely of Phylosophicall, but even of vulgar and common medicines
observations.note: They know neither the philosophical nor even the common medicines.

observations.quote: who disdaining the writings of the Ancients
observations.note: They are blamed for scorning the writings of the Ancients.

observations.quote: These men get their knowledge piece-meale out of men, & gaine their experience by the death of others
observations.note: The note says the false practitioners learn piecemeal from men and gain experience by others' deaths.

observations.quote: I know not what Secrets and Experiences they trust to
observations.note: The author says he does not know what Secrets and Experiences they rely on.

observations.quote: before they scarce know how to put fire into the furnace
observations.note: They undertake the gravest cures before they can so much as fire a furnace.

observations.quote: or else cure the party and his disease at once with a turse of the Church-yard
observations.note: 'Cure' is not meant plainly: patient and disease are ended together, with something of the church-yard.

observations.quote: all the Medicines both of the Arabians and Grecians, are desperate and without hope of doing any good
observations.note: In great diseases the medicines of the Arabians and Grecians sometimes fail altogether.

observations.quote: many times the cure is left to the absurd Remedies of Old Wives and Empericks to the great dishonour and ignominy of Physitians
observations.note: The cure is then often left to old wives and Empericks, to the physicians' shame.

observations.quote: these circumforaneous and adulterous Theophrasteans, with their unlawfully prepared Remedies
observations.note: The false Theophrasteans are named again, their remedies called unlawfully prepared.

observations.quote: doe sometime exceed many Galenists in many great and perilous diseases
observations.note: The author grants that these men sometimes do better than many Galenists.

observations.quote: yet no conscientious man will ever approve their uncertaine, bold, rash, dangerous, impious practice of Physick
observations.note: Even so their practice is condemned: it endangers the sick by doubtful experiments.

observations.quote: No rabble of Physitians in the City is more numerous then these.
observations.note: No crowd of physicians in the City is larger than these.
